claims.text: Multiphase refractory high-entropy alloys containing W, Ta, Mo, Nb, V, or Ti will undergo a ductile-brittle-ductile transition during aging at 500–800 °C.
The initial ductile state is governed by a disordered BCC solid solution.
Formation of B2 or L12 ordered phases or spinodal decomposition during aging produces an intermediate brittle state.
Ordering causes brittleness by restricting dislocation mobility and increasing Peierls stress.
Further aging restores ductility through precipitate coarsening or precipitation of ductile secondary phases.
The proposed transition depends on ordering kinetics and the stability of the ordered phase relative to the matrix.
The starting W-Ta-Mo-Nb-V or W-Ta-Mo-Nb-V-Ti alloy has a disordered BCC or BCC+B2 matrix.
The starting alloy has a grain size below 50 µm.
The starting alloy contains no pre-existing ordered precipitates.
Coherent or semi-coherent ordered precipitates increase critical resolved shear stress and promote planar slip, producing localized strain and brittle fracture.
Precipitate coarsening lowers obstacle density and thereby restores plasticity.

Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces in a tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve crack-initiating stress concentrations while retaining tensile ductility.
The Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy developed an HCP phase after HIP and was highly brittle in tensile testing.
The cited HCP-phase result supports ordering-induced embrittlement in BCC refractory alloys.
Elongation to failure will fall to a minimum after roughly 100–500 hours and recover after more than 1000 hours of aging.
The ductility minimum will coincide with the peak volume fraction of ordered precipitates.
Yield strength will peak before the ductility minimum.
In single-phase alloys, standard aging behavior consists of monotonically increasing strength and monotonically decreasing ductility due to precipitation hardening.
The transition occurs only where there is sufficient thermodynamic driving force for ordering and enough diffusion without immediate phase dissolution or melting.

The hypothesis is falsified by monotonic ductility loss without recovery, lack of correlation between the brittle minimum and ordered-phase volume fraction, or failure to detect ordered phases after aging.

contradictions.description: The initial ductile state is attributed specifically to a disordered BCC solid solution, but the allowed initial state also includes a BCC+B2 matrix; B2 is chemically ordered and could alter the proposed initial mechanism.

Ordered coherent or semi-coherent precipitates are proposed to impede dislocations and cause brittleness, while the cited coherent-nanoprecipitation rationale says coherent interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission, relieve stress concentrations, and preserve ductility. No conditions are given to reconcile these opposite effects.
